segments.voice: A delegation from home stands at the door. They've traveled a long way, to a temple town by the sea on the far western coast. They've been sent to bring a woman back, and they aren't supposed to return without her. She listens. She doesn't say no. She asks for one thing first: let me go to the temple once more. The town is Dwarka, the city tradition gives to Krishna in his later life. The woman is Mira, and today, our last day with her, is the story tradition tells of how her road ended.
screen: `A DELEGATION AT THE DOOR.` → `DWARKA, BY THE SEA.` → `HOW HER ROAD ENDED.`

segments.voice: This is tradition's story, in paraphrase. After Vrindavan, Mira travels on to Dwarka, the city of Krishna as a king, where he is worshipped in the temple as Ranchhod. Back in Mewar, things have gone badly, and some tellings say the royal house comes to believe its troubles began when Mira was driven out. So messengers are sent to bring her home. They plead; some tellings say they threaten to fast until she agrees. Mira asks only to go into the temple first, to take leave of her Lord. She goes in, and she doesn't come out. Tradition says she merged into the image of Krishna, and that her sari was found wrapped around it. Why ask to go in first? Because for a devotee, the image in that temple isn't a statue of Krishna. It's a murti, and Hindus believe that once a murti is installed and invited with prayer, the Lord is present in it. That's why temples wake the deity at dawn, bathe him, dress him and offer him food. Mira wasn't saying goodbye to a building. She was taking leave of her Lord, the way you'd hold someone before a long trip. And the tradition tells what happened next as union, not death. Andal's story, a few days ago, ends almost the same way, at Srirangam. Two women, two languages, and both go into the shrine to the Lord who is there. That is why, in many Hindu homes today, people stop at the shrine before a long trip: you take leave of someone who is there.
screen: `MESSENGERS SENT TO DWARKA` · `ONE LAST VISIT, ONLY HER SARI LEFT` · `THE LORD IS PRESENT IN THE MURTI` · `UNION, LIKE ANDAL AT SRIRANGAM`

segments.voice: Many Hindu families bow to the home shrine before they leave the house, and again when they come back: palms together, darshan, seeing the Lord and being seen. If there's a murti or a picture near you, stand before it and greet it as someone present, not an object, and say where you're going today. If you don't pray, pause at your door and bring to mind who you'll come home to.

1360.title: The silkworm's house

segments.voice: A silkworm doesn't find its house. It makes it, out of its own body, thread by thread, turning and turning, until the house is finished and the worm is sealed inside. Everything it needed came from within it, and so did the trap. That small, exact picture opens one of the sayings of a woman people called Akka, elder sister. She spoke to Shiva in Kannada, in the south, and her name for him was a flower.
screen: `A SILKWORM SPINS ITS HOUSE.` → `AKKA, ELDER SISTER.` → `HER NAME FOR GOD WAS A FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Her name is Mahadevi, and people called her Akka, elder sister, so she comes down to us as Akka Mahadevi. She belongs to the Virashaiva, or Lingayat, saints of Karnataka, devotees of Shiva who spoke their faith in short, sharp sayings called vachanas. They're closer to speech than hymns, in plain Kannada. Her sayings carry her name for Shiva: Chennamallikarjuna. Some readers render it as the beautiful lord, white as jasmine: a god called by the name of a small white flower. The silkworm, in paraphrase. The silkworm builds its house lovingly out of itself, and dies tangled in what it wound. So I burn with my heart's wanting. Lord white as jasmine, cut through this greed in me, and show me a way out. Notice first: she doesn't blame the world for trapping her. The thread comes from inside, her own wanting, spun round and round. That's an old Hindu teaching, said plainly: what binds us is our own desire. And notice second: she doesn't free herself. She asks Shiva to cut the thread. His devotees call that freeing gift his grace, anugraha, one of the five acts the tradition gives him. So the saying holds both halves of the faith at once: I spun this, and I need the Lord to free me. Then listen to the voice. No priest stands between her and Shiva, no special language. A woman speaks in her own tongue to a god she calls by the name of a flower.
screen: `AKKA, ELDER SISTER, SAINT OF SHIVA` · `THE LORD WHITE AS JASMINE` · `THE THREAD COMES FROM INSIDE` · `ASKING HIM TO CUT IT`

segments.voice: Notice one wanting active in you right now, a snack, a message, a result. Don't fight it or follow it; watch it spin like a silkworm turning. Devotees of Shiva often repeat his five-syllable mantra, namah shivaya. If you pray, say it softly on each out-breath and ask him, as Akka did, to cut the thread. If you don't, loosen your grip a little with each breath out.

segments.voice: A gathering of saints in the city of Kalyana, where people come to talk about God plainly, and to be tested. In walks a young woman who has left a king's house. She has given up her clothes on the road; her long hair is all that covers her. Before she can sit, one of the saints, known for his searching questions, asks her something that would make anyone flinch. Her answer is what the story keeps. Today: the walk from the palace, and the test at the door.
screen: `A GATHERING OF SAINTS.` → `ONLY HER HAIR.` → `A QUESTION AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Her tradition's story, in paraphrase. A local king, Kaushika, wants Mahadevi. The tellings differ on what happens next: some say she refuses him, some that she marries him on conditions he goes on to break. Either way, she leaves. Her husband, she says, is the lord white as jasmine, and she has no use for one who dies and decays. She walks away from the palace, sheds her clothes, and goes on, covered by her hair. She comes to Kalyana, where the Virashaiva saints gather around Basavanna in a hall the tradition calls the Anubhava Mantapa, the hall of experience. The name is the teaching. Anubhava means experience: these saints, the sharanas, asked whether you had truly met Shiva, not what caste you were born to or whether you were a woman. There Allama Prabhu, a teacher famous in the stories for his hard questions, tests her. He asks, roughly: if you've truly given up the body's shame, why hide behind your hair? Her answer comes in more than one form. In one, she says that until the fruit is ripe, the skin doesn't fall away. In another, that the covering is for the people looking, so the sight of her won't trouble them. She doesn't claim to be finished; she says she's ripening. And she thinks of the people around her, not only her own freedom. The saints don't send her away. Tradition says they welcome her, and call her Akka, elder sister. In the hall of experience, an honest not yet was enough.
screen: `SHE LEAVES THE KING'S HOUSE` · `THE HALL OF EXPERIENCE` · `ALLAMA'S HARD QUESTION` · `UNTIL THE FRUIT IS RIPE`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where you're not finished yet, a habit, a hurt, a hope, and without scolding it or pretending it's done, say quietly to yourself: still ripening. Breathe in and let it be unfinished; breathe out and let it grow in its own time. If you pray, you can offer the unripe part to God as it is.
Akka Mahadevi. She left a king for the lord white as jasmine, came to Kalyana in only her hair, and answered Allama's test: until the fruit is ripe, the skin stays on.

segments.voice: A woman goes from house to house with her hands held out, a wandering seeker begging for her food. What's strange is what she asks for. She doesn't ask God to soften the hearts behind the doors. She asks for the doors to give her nothing. If they do give, she asks for the food to fall. And if it falls, something stranger still. Our last day with Akka Mahadevi: one short poem, and a request that runs backward.
screen: `HOUSE TO HOUSE, HANDS OUT.` → `SHE ASKS FOR NOTHING.` → `A REQUEST THAT RUNS BACKWARD.`

segments.voice: Here is the vachana, in paraphrase. Make me go from house to house, hands held out for alms. If I beg, let them give me nothing. If they give, let it fall to the ground. If it falls, before I can pick it up, let a dog come and take it, O lord white as jasmine. It works like a staircase going down. Each line takes away one more thing to lean on: the comfort of home, the kindness of strangers, the food already in her hand, even the chance to stoop and pick it up. At the bottom there's nothing left to hold, and the last words are his name. The poem doesn't end on the dog. It ends on the lord white as jasmine. Her tradition, the Lingayat or Virashaiva way of Karnataka, calls its saints sharanas: those who have taken refuge, in Shiva alone. This poem is that word lived all the way down, every support stripped away but one. Some readers also hear honesty: she knows how easily a full plate becomes the thing she trusts. So she asks to be emptied, all the way, until the only thing in her hands is him. The poem never says she starves, and it never asks anyone else to live this way. And there's a small surprise at the bottom of the stairs. A hungry dog eats. Even her emptiness feeds someone. Three days with Akka: a silkworm caught in its own threads, a hard question at the door of the saints, and a woman asking for her hands to stay open.

segments.voice: Dinner is served, and the young wife's plate looks generous, a full mound of rice. Only she knows what's underneath: a stone, with the rice spread thin over it, so the plate looks full while there's hardly anything to eat. Kashmiris tell this story about a young bride named Lalla and the mother-in-law who, tradition says, served her this way. She doesn't complain. She eats what there is, washes the stone, and sets it back. In time she would leave that house and become the poet Kashmir remembers as Lal Ded.
screen: `A FULL PLATE OF RICE.` → `A STONE UNDERNEATH.` → `THE BRIDE WHO BECAME LAL DED.`

segments.voice: She goes by more than one name: Lalla, Lalleshwari, and Lal Ded, the one Kashmir knows best. She sang in Kashmiri, not Sanskrit, in short sayings called vakhs, easy to remember and pass from mouth to mouth. The stories say that after years of hardship at home she walked out as a wandering seeker, and found a teacher. Then comes a saying about that teacher, in paraphrase. My teacher gave me only one word. He said: from outside, go within. That one word became my rule, and so I began to dance, with nothing on. Notice how little she was given. Not a library, not a long course of rituals. One word. That's still how many Hindus receive a path: from a guru, at initiation, diksha, often as one short word or mantra, given in person and kept for life. And she didn't argue with it or add to it. She took it all the way. If what matters is within, then the outside, even the clothes, stops being the point. segments.voice: Yesterday, Lal Ded: the bride with a stone under her rice, and the one word her teacher gave her, from outside, go within.
screen: `LAL DED.`

segments.voice: A cup shaped from wet clay and dried in the sun, but never fired in a kiln. It looks like a cup. It holds its shape. Pour water in, though, and the sides darken. Drop by drop, the water soaks into the clay and seeps away, and the cup begins to soften. In one saying Lal Ded uses that kind of cup to describe herself, next to an even shakier picture: a boat, a whole sea, and a rope of loose thread.
screen: `A CUP OF UNBAKED CLAY.` → `THE WATER SEEPS AWAY.` → `A BOAT ON A ROPE OF THREAD.`

segments.voice: Here is the vakh, in paraphrase. With a rope of loose, untwisted thread, I am hauling a boat across the sea. If only God would hear me and carry me over. Like water in cups of unbaked clay, I am seeping away. How I long to go home. First the rope. Towing a heavy boat across the sea with untwisted thread is close to hopeless. The rope is whatever she has to pull with: her effort, her discipline, her practice. She doesn't pretend it's strong. Then the prayer in the middle: if only God would hear me. She isn't boasting that she's arrived. She's asking to be carried. Many readers hear in her sea one of Hinduism's oldest pictures: samsara, life after life, as an ocean, and God as the one who carries you across. Then the cup, her life draining away a little each day, the way water leaves unfired clay. Then the last word, home. Not the house she left. Some Shaiva readers in Kashmir hear the self finding its way back to Shiva, its true home; some hear, more simply, the ache to be where you belong. And notice the honesty. The woman who danced free on one word says plainly: my rope is weak, my time is leaking, I may not make it across on my own. The tradition kept this saying. It didn't polish it into a victory. It let a saint say she was struggling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lal Ded hauled a boat with a rope of loose thread, seeping away like water in unbaked clay, and still longed for home.
screen: `LAL DED.`

segments.voice: A length of cloth, torn into two equal strips, one over each shoulder. That's how one Kashmiri story has Lal Ded walking through town. Every time someone mocks her, she ties a knot in one strip. Every time someone bows and praises her, she ties a knot in the other. By evening both are full of knots. Then, the story says, she has them weighed. They weigh exactly the same. It's a story told about her, not one she told. But she has a saying that sounds just like it.
screen: `TWO STRIPS OF CLOTH.` → `A KNOT FOR EACH INSULT, A KNOT FOR EACH BOW.` → `THEY WEIGH THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Here is the vakh, in paraphrase. Let them curse me, let them jeer at me. Let each one say whatever pleases them. Let the good come and worship me with flowers. What does any of it gain them? I remain untouched. The first time through, it can sound cold, as if she doesn't care about anyone. Look again. She isn't telling the mockers to stop, and she isn't refusing the flowers. She lets both come. What she won't do is let either one decide who she is. The insult doesn't shrink her. The garland doesn't swell her. That's the knot story in a few lines: praise and blame, on the same scale, weigh the same. This was no small thing for a woman who had left her husband's house and walked about as a wandering seeker; tradition says she drew plenty of both. Hindus have a name for this. The Bhagavad Gita calls evenness of mind samatva, and says that evenness is yoga; later it calls the one dear to Krishna the same in honor and dishonor, with friend and foe. Lal Ded's saying is samatva in her own Kashmiri words, on her own street. And the week looks back: Mirabai, then three days with Akka Mahadevi, and three with Lal Ded: one word, go within; a rope of loose thread; two strips of cloth that weigh the same. Different languages, each woman in words of her own.
